<div class="clt-lesson batch-lesson" data-lesson="assumptions"><h2 id="learning-goals">What are we trying to understand?</h2><p><strong>How sensitive are conclusions to an unusual observation or a change in analysis?</strong></p><p>Compare two independent groups of six illustrative attention scores. Change one score and compare mean-based Welch inference with a rank-based exact permutation analysis. These methods do not necessarily answer identical questions.</p><div class="clt-overview"><strong>Learning goals</strong><ol><li>Recognize that assumptions belong to the design and statistical model.</li><li>Investigate sensitivity to unusual observations.</li><li>Compare mean-based and rank-based analyses without treating them as interchangeable.</li><li>Explain transparent reporting of sensitivity analyses.</li></ol></div><h2 id="explore">Make a prediction and explore</h2><section class="clt-simulator"><p>Predict whether increasing an already high score always makes a mean comparison more statistically significant.</p><div class="controls"><div><label for="extreme">Selected observation in group B: <output id="extreme-v">60</output></label><input id="extreme" type="range" min="58" max="100" step="1" value="60"></div></div><div class="metrics"><div class="metric"><span>Mean difference B − A</span><strong id="difference">—</strong></div><div class="metric"><span>Median difference B − A</span><strong id="median-diff">—</strong></div><div class="metric"><span>Welch p-value</span><strong id="p">—</strong></div><div class="metric"><span>Rank permutation p-value</span><strong id="rank-p">—</strong></div></div><div id="chart" class="plot"></div><table class="data-table"><caption>Group summaries</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Statistic</th><th scope="col">Group A</th><th scope="col">Group B</th></tr></thead><tbody id="summary"></tbody></table><p id="ci" role="status"></p><p id="rank-detail"></p><details><summary>View scores</summary><p id="data"></p></details></section><h2 id="interpret">Interpret what you find</h2><ol><li>Record the results at selected score 60, 80 and 100. Compare the mean difference, SD and Welch p-value.</li><li>Explain why the rank-based p-value does not change when the selected score remains the largest observation.</li><li>Identify assumptions about independence and the data-generating process that cannot be verified by a plot.</li><li>Write a two-sentence sensitivity report without deleting the observation merely to obtain significance.</li></ol><h2 id="explanation">What is the method telling us?</h2><p>Welch’s t-test compares means and does not require equal variances. With six observations per group, strong skew or unusual values can undermine its approximate reference distribution. The rank-based demonstration computes all 924 possible allocations of six observations to one group, and compares the absolute difference in mean pooled ranks. Under an exchangeable null (identical distributions and independent observations), this is an exact permutation test. It is not a general test of equal medians; different spread or shape may affect interpretation.</p><div class="formula">First check study design and independence. Inspect distributions and unusual observations. Identify the estimand. Compare reasonable methods transparently, rather than choosing whichever produces the smallest p-value.</div><p>For related observations, analyze differences and consider paired methods such as Wilcoxon signed-rank when its assumptions fit. For several independent groups, Kruskal–Wallis is a possible rank-based alternative to ANOVA. These alternatives are introduced conceptually here, not implemented. Never infer that assumptions are satisfied solely because a diagnostic test is nonsignificant.</p><h2 id="knowledge-check">Check your understanding</h2><p>Choose an answer, then check your reasoning.
